items.assessment: Transient focal weakness and aphasia retain urgent TIA/stroke significance despite resolution; risk review and a diary do not replace acute assessment.
Abrupt diplopia with imbalance distinguishes a central posterior-circulation concern from peripheral vertigo even with equal hand strength.
A maximal-at-onset headache unlike established migraine warrants emergency evaluation; prior rescue treatment cannot establish the cause.
Serial decline in arousal with repeated vomiting after trauma outweighs the initial normal examination and symptomatic antiemetic care.
Observed comprehension of unmodelled instructions and factual responses supports preserved comprehension with effortful expression; motor articulation is distinguished.
New arousal, focal motor and pupil changes are selected; unchanged pre-existing findings are reasonable comparison controls.
Plan-directed rescue and airway support are correct; oral medicine, waiting and restarting the seizure clock are basic safety distinctions. Relabel foundation.
issues: Plan-directed rescue and airway support are correct; oral medicine, waiting and restarting the seizure clock are basic safety distinctions. Relabel foundation.

items.assessment: Failure to recover between recurrent convulsions distinguishes an ongoing emergency from ordinary postictal recovery.
Improving mentation and regular breathing support recovery; focal deficit, renewed convulsions and declining arousal require review.
The keyed event record includes onset, automatisms, responsiveness, duration and subsequent amnesia without attributing intent.
New bulbar weakness, ineffective cough and fatigue threaten airway protection/ventilation despite unchanged ocular or limb findings.
Serial vital capacity directly assesses ventilatory reserve in GBS; saturation and rate alone can miss respiratory muscle deterioration.
Marked cardiovascular fluctuations fit possible dysautonomia and justify ongoing ordered monitoring; one normal reading is insufficient.
Baseline neurological assessment and infection investigation are appropriate during fever-associated worsening; later reassessment must not replace the initial assessment.
The supplied high spinal injury, headache, marked hypertension and catheter kink fit dysreflexia; explanation includes upright positioning and trigger relief.
New saddle sensory change with retention and back pain identifies time-sensitive cauda equina concern rather than an isolated urinary problem.
New bilateral motor and bladder dysfunction is distinctly more urgent than unchanged sensory deficits or responding common postoperative symptoms.
Fever, meningeal symptoms and declining arousal support urgent CNS infection assessment; migraine alone does not explain the full pattern.
Avoiding nasal instrumentation/packing and not treating glucose strips as diagnostic are defensible CSF-leak precautions; classify this direct safety knowledge foundation.
issues: Avoiding nasal instrumentation/packing and not treating glucose strips as diagnostic are defensible CSF-leak precautions; classify this direct safety knowledge foundation.

Urgent assessment of transient monocular visual loss is defensible, but the attached NEI retinal-detachment page does not directly support the transient ischaemic premise. Add a targeted source.

proposedChanges.stem: A client develops new flashes, many floaters and a shadow spreading across one eye's vision, without pain. Which complication most urgently needs to be excluded?
why: Angle closure more often causes severe eye pain, halos and systemic symptoms.
Migraine can cause transient visual phenomena, but a new progressive monocular shadow with flashes and floaters requires retinal assessment.
Cataract usually causes gradual visual change rather than a sudden field shadow with flashes.
This painless acute pattern requires urgent ophthalmic evaluation for a retinal tear or detachment.

proposedChanges.stem: After prolonged diarrhoea has stopped, potassium remains 2.9 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) despite prescribed replacement. Magnesium is 0.40 mmol/L (reference 0.70–1.00). Which identified abnormality may help explain the poor potassium response?
options: Magnesium depletion promoting continued renal potassium loss
A recent fluid load diluting the serum potassium
An insulin-related shift of potassium into cells
A newly increasing gastrointestinal potassium loss
why: Marked magnesium depletion can make potassium difficult to correct and warrants coordinated replacement and monitoring.
Dilution is a possible cause in some settings, but it is not an identified contributor in the supplied findings.
Insulin can shift potassium, but there is no evidence here of a new insulin exposure; magnesium depletion is demonstrated.
The reported diarrhoea has stopped; ongoing magnesium depletion is the identified abnormality requiring attention.

items.assessment: Seizure with sodium116 is an emergency; controlled correction is appropriately protocol based with airway protection already initiated.
The question uses individual prescribed correction limits and multi-system response rather than inventing a universal sodium correction rate.
Insulin redistribution can reveal a whole-body potassium deficit in DKA; the explanation distinguishes serum concentration from stores.
Persistent ketones/acidosis despite glucose improvement justify continued protocol insulin with glucose support as indicated; transition criteria are not oversimplified.
Given glucose42/osmolality338 and little acidosis, HHS is the most compatible concern; the rationale appropriately allows overlap.
Large dilute losses and rising sodium after pituitary surgery justify prompt DI assessment; daily weight alone is too slow for rapid losses.
Foundation classification is appropriate for accounting for milk/IV carriers/ice in a supplied total-fluid plan, without defining unauthorized amounts.
Severe multisystem hyperthyroid deterioration during infection supports thyroid-storm concern and does not deny the infection trigger.
Depressed ventilation and arousal take priority over medication reconciliation, warming and confirmatory sampling in severe hypothyroid decline.
The adrenal crisis key is defensible, but adding sole explanation to septic shock advertises the wrong option. Remove that qualifier.
issues: The adrenal crisis key is defensible, but adding sole explanation to septic shock advertises the wrong option. Remove that qualifier.

items.assessment: Positional loss of drainage with suprapubic discomfort supports checking the mechanical pathway before fluid loading or renal tests.
High post-obstructive output plus falling potassium or symptomatic hypotension indicates losses; resolved discomfort does not establish balance.
Pain and cloudy peritoneal effluent warrant prompt dialysis contact and aseptic sampling; waiting for a subsequent bag could delay care.
New absent thrill and bruit after reassessment raise possible access failure; exercise or oral-fluid review cannot establish restored flow.
Initial-dialysis headache/vomiting/confusion with measured normal glucose and stable pressure support prompt disequilibrium assessment without definitive nursing diagnosis.
Fever/chills and worsening pain with a stone raise infected obstruction concern; routine passage advice does not address source control.
Cola urine, oedema, hypertension and oliguria support a glomerular pattern; hydration advice alone would misread retention.
Renal decline and rising potassium with rhythm change are meaningful rhabdomyolysis complications; pain or urine colour improvement is not proof of recovery.
Diuretic AKI recovery can precede restored concentration/clearance; volume and electrolyte monitoring remain necessary.
Rebound potassium and delayed hypoglycaemia are valid reasons for follow-up, but only/every qualifiers make distractors trivial. Use competing mechanisms.
issues: Rebound potassium and delayed hypoglycaemia are valid reasons for follow-up, but only/every qualifiers make distractors trivial. Use competing mechanisms.

options: The potassium shift can reverse, and insulin action may outlast the supplied glucose
The potassium fall shows increased urinary elimination, while glucose loss causes hypoglycaemia
The fall reflects permanent potassium binding, while glucose raises the measured potassium
The potassium shift persists until dialysis, while glucose correction determines its duration
why: Insulin shifts potassium into cells without removing it; potassium may rebound and delayed hypoglycaemia remains possible, requiring protocol monitoring.
Insulin does not directly restore renal potassium elimination; glucose uptake, rather than urinary loss alone, contributes to hypoglycaemia.
Insulin is not a potassium-binding treatment, and the explanation does not account for its cellular actions.
Redistribution can reverse before definitive elimination, and potassium follow-up is not determined solely by the glucose result.
